props.title: Love Story

sections.content: Love Story (1970) defined the tragic romance genre for a generation, introducing the infamous line "Love means never having to say you're sorry." The film's stark simplicity - privileged Harvard student Oliver Barrett IV falls for working-class Jenny Cavalleri - created a template countless romances would follow. Director Arthur Hiller stripped away melodramatic excess, letting Ryan O'Neal and Ali MacGraw's chemistry drive the narrative. The film's influence echoes through later tragic romances like The Notebook (2004) and A Walk to Remember (2002), though few matched its raw emotional impact.

sections.content: The success of Love Story launched a wave of tragic romances in the 1970s. The Other Side of Midnight (1977) amplified the melodrama with a globe-spanning tale of obsession. Bobby Deerfield (1977) paired Al Pacino with a terminally ill European woman. These films established dying young as the ultimate romantic tragedy - a trope that would reach its commercial peak with Titanic (1997) and influence contemporary tearjerkers like The Fault in Our Stars (2014).

Love Story's class conflict narrative particularly resonated in early 1970s America. While Pretty Woman (1990) would later give the wealthy man/working class woman dynamic a fairy tale ending, Love Story used it to underscore life's cruel randomness. This influenced later films like An Officer and a Gentleman (1982) and Endless Love (1981) that explored how class differences complicate romance. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Romance Films

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond tragic love stories. Its stripped-down narrative style - focusing intensely on the central couple while minimizing subplots - influenced romantic dramas like Before Sunrise (1995) and Once (2007). Even romantic comedies like 500 Days of Summer (2009) borrowed its non-traditional structure and bittersweet tone.
